Visible
VIZ-i-bl
adj. (able to be seen; perceptible to the eye)
Greek horatos, able to be seen, from horao, to see. Latin visibilis, from videre, to see. Paul pairs it with its negative, aoratos, invisible, to make a statement about the totality of creation.

Biblical Definition

For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him. The pairing visible and invisible is doing a specific job: it closes every gap. Paul is not listing two categories of thing but using a pair of opposites to mean everything, and he reinforces it three times in one sentence — all things, in heaven and in earth, by him and for him. The four terms that follow are names for angelic and spiritual ranks, and their inclusion is the point of the verse in its setting. The Colossian error involved the worship of angels and an interest in intermediary powers; Paul answers by putting every such power on the created side of the line, made by Christ and made for him. Nothing in the unseen realm is uncreated, and nothing is outside his ownership. The preceding verse has already established who is speaking of: who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature — and firstborn here is a title of rank and heirship, not of origin, since the one by whom all things were created cannot himself be among the things created. The verse following completes the claim: and he is before all things, and by him all things consist. John says the same at the beginning of his Gospel: all things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): perceivable by the eye; that can be seen; apparent; open; conspicuous.

expand to see more

VISIBLE, a. Perceivable by the eye; that can be seen; as, the sun and stars are visible.

VISIBLE, a. Apparent; open; conspicuous; as the visible church.

INVISIBLE, a. That cannot be seen; imperceptible by the sight.

CREATE, v.t. To produce; to bring into being from nothing; to cause to exist.

DOMINION, n. Sovereign or supreme authority; the power of governing and controlling; an order of angels.

Key Scripture

Colossians 1:16 — "For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:"

Colossians 1:15 — "Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature:"

Colossians 1:17 — "And he is before all things, and by him all things consist."

John 1:3 — "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made."

Modern Corruption

The deity of Christ is denied by reading firstborn as first-created, and the unseen realm is either dismissed as mythology or treated as a field for speculation; Paul places all of it on the created side and under Christ.

expand to see more

Arianism in its ancient and modern forms rests on the firstborn of every creature, read as though Christ were the first item in the list of created things. Verse 16 refutes it in the next breath: by him were ALL things created, and a creator of all things is not one of them. Prototokos in Scripture denotes rank and inheritance rather than sequence — David is called God's firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth, and he was the youngest of eight sons. Nicaea confessed what this passage teaches: begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father. The dictionary holds the eternal generation of the Son and the full deity of Christ without reservation.

On the unseen realm there are two failures and the text answers both. The materialist reading treats thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers as first-century mythology, which requires deleting a great deal of the New Testament. The opposite failure is the fascination Colossae itself displayed — an appetite for angelic hierarchies, intermediaries, and the mapping of spiritual ranks, which recurs in every generation that finds ordinary doctrine dull. Paul's handling is the model: he affirms that the powers are real, names them, and then makes the only point that matters about them. They were made by Christ and for Christ, and the believer who is in him has nothing to negotiate with them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek horatos (G3707), visible; aoratos (G517), invisible; prototokos (G4416), firstborn; sunistemi (G4921), to hold together or consist.

expand to see more

Greek horatos (G3707) — able to be seen; rendered visible, its only occurrence.

Greek aoratos (G517) — unseen, invisible; used of God himself in the previous verse.

Greek prototokos (G4416) — firstborn; a title of rank and heirship, not of origin.

Greek ktizo (G2936) — to create; the verb whose subject is Christ and whose object is all things.

Greek sunistemi (G4921) — to hold together; by him all things consist.

Usage

"“visible and invisible” — a pair of opposites meaning everything."

"“thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers” — the unseen ranks, created."

"“all things were created by him, and for him” — the claim stated twice."
